en: Majjhima Nikāya 101,
the Devadaha Sutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at a town of the Sakyans named Devadaha.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“There are, bhikkhus, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:”
‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
Thus, through the exhaustion of old kamma by means of asceticism and the non-performance of new kamma, there is no further influx in the future;

with no further influx in the future, there is the destruction of kamma; with the destruction of kamma, the destruction of suffering; with the destruction of suffering, the destruction of feeling; and with the destruction of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.’
“Bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas speak thus.
When I have approached the Nigaṇṭhas who speak thus, bhikkhus, I say to them:
‘Is it true, friends Nigaṇṭhas, that you speak thus and hold such a view?’”
‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
Thus, through the exhaustion of old kamma by means of asceticism (tapas) and the non-performance of new kamma, there will be no influx in the future;

with no influx in the future, there is the destruction of kamma; with the destruction of kamma, the destruction of suffering; with the destruction of suffering, the destruction of feeling; and with the destruction of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.’”
And when those Nigaṇṭhas, monks, were thus questioned by me, they admitted, “Yes.
I then said to them:
“But do you, friends Nigaṇṭhas, know this?”
‘Did we exist before, and it is not that we did not exist?
‘No indeed, friend.
‘Then do you know, friends Nigaṇṭhas, [who we were]?’
‘Did we ourselves previously perform evil kamma, and not fail to do so?
‘Indeed not, friend.
‘But then, friends Nigaṇṭhas, do you know this:’
‘Did we perform such and such an evil deed?
‘No indeed, friend.
‘But then, friends Nigaṇṭhas, do you know:’
‘Has so much suffering been worn away? Or so much suffering remains to be worn away? Or when so much suffering has been worn away, will all suffering have been worn away?
‘Not so, friend.
‘But then, friends Nigaṇṭhas, do you know—’
‘The abandoning of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states in this very life’?
“Certainly not, friend.
“So it seems, friend Nigaṇṭhas, that you do not know—”
"You do not know: 'We indeed existed in the past;
we did not not exist. You do not know: 'We indeed performed evil kamma in the past;
we did not not perform it. You do not know: 'We performed such and such evil kamma.'"

"You do not know: 'This much suffering has been worn away,' or 'this much suffering remains to be worn away,' or 'when this much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away'—that is, the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states in this very life.
This being so, it is not fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to make such a declaration."
“Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
Thus, through the exhaustion of old kamma by means of asceticism (tapas) and the non-performance of new kamma, there is no further influx in the future;

with no further influx in the future, there is the destruction of kamma; with the destruction of kamma, there is the destruction of suffering; with the destruction of suffering, there is the destruction of feeling; and with the destruction of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”
But if you, friends Nigaṇṭhas, were to know:
"We indeed existed in the past, we did not not exist," and if you were to know:
"We indeed performed evil kamma in the past, we did not not perform it," and if you were to know...
‘We have performed such and such evil karma,’ you would know:
‘This much suffering has been exhausted, this much suffering remains to be exhausted, and when this much suffering has been exhausted, all suffering will have been exhausted. You would know:
‘In this very life, there is the abandoning of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states.’
This being so, it would be appropriate for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:
"Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
Thus, through the exhaustion of old kamma by means of asceticism and the non-performance of new kamma, there is no influx for the future."

"In the future, there will be no further influx [of kamma]; with the exhaustion of kamma, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.
"Friends, Nigaṇṭhas, it is just as if a man were pierced by an arrow smeared with a potent poison;
he would experience painful, sharp, and bitter sensations on account of the piercing of that arrow."
His friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relatives would bring a physician and a surgeon to attend to him.
That physician and surgeon would cut open the opening of the wound with a blade;
because of that cutting of the opening of the wound with the blade, he would experience painful, intense, and bitter sensations.
That physician, a surgeon, would probe for the arrow with a probe;
because of probing for the arrow with the probe, he would experience painful, sharp, and bitter sensations.
Then that physician, a surgeon, would extract the arrow.
He might experience painful, intense, and bitter sensations due to the probing of the arrow.
Then that physician, the surgeon, might apply a caustic substance to the opening of the wound;
he might experience painful, intense, and bitter sensations due to the application of the caustic substance to the opening of the wound.
Then, at a later time, when the wound had healed and was covered with skin, he would be healthy, happy, independent, self-governing, and able to go wherever he wished.
It would occur to him:
"Formerly, I was pierced by an arrow that was poisoned and smeared with a thick coating."
Thus, for the sake of extracting that arrow, I experienced painful, sharp, and bitter sensations.
My friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relations brought a physician, a surgeon, to attend to me.
That physician, the surgeon, cut open the opening of the wound with a blade.
Thus, because the surgeon cut around the opening of the wound, I experienced painful, intense, and bitter sensations.
Then that physician, the surgeon, probed for the arrow with a probe;
because of that probing for the arrow with the probe, I experienced painful, intense, and bitter sensations.
That physician, the surgeon, extracted the arrow from me;
because of that extraction of the arrow, I experienced feelings that were painful, sharp, and bitter.
That physician, the surgeon, then applied a medicinal caustic to the opening of my wound.
“Thus, friend Nigaṇṭhas, because of having had that medicinal coal applied to the opening of my wound, I experienced painful, sharp, and bitter sensations.
But now, with the wound healed and covered over, I am healthy, happy, independent, self-mastering, and able to go wherever I wish.
In the same way, friends, if you were to know:
"You would know: 'We indeed existed in the past, we did not not exist';
you would know: 'We indeed performed evil kamma in the past, we did not not perform it';
you would know: 'We performed such and such evil kamma.'"

Or that "this much suffering has been worn away, this much suffering remains to be worn away, or when this much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away"—if you could know this, then it would be appropriate for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:
"In this very life, there is the abandoning of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states.
But since this is not so, [it is not appropriate].
“Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
Thus, through the exhaustion of old kamma by means of asceticism (tapas) and the non-performance of new kamma, there is no further influx for the future;

with no further influx for the future, there is the destruction of kamma; with the destruction of kamma, there is the destruction of suffering; with the destruction of suffering, there is the destruction of feeling; and with the destruction of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”
But because you, friends Nigaṇṭhas, do not know—"We indeed existed in the past;
we did not not exist"—and because you do not know—"We indeed performed evil kamma in the past; we did not not perform it"—and because you do not know—
"You do not know, 'We have done such and such an evil deed,' nor do you know,

'This much suffering has been exhausted, this much suffering remains to be exhausted, or when this much suffering has been exhausted, all suffering will have been exhausted'; nor do you know, 'In this very life,
there is the abandoning of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states.'"
Therefore, it is not appropriate for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:
"Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
Thus, through the exhaustion of old kamma by means of asceticism and the non-performance of new kamma, there is no influx in the future."

‘In the future there will be no further influx [of karma]; with the exhaustion of karma comes the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering comes the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.
When this was said, monks, those Nigaṇṭhas said this to me: ‘Friend, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is omniscient and all-seeing; he claims a knowledge and vision that is entirely exhaustive.’”
“Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously established before me.
He said this:
“Friends, Nigaṇṭhas, you have indeed committed evil deeds in the past; exhaust them by means of this bitter practice of asceticism.”
But that which here now consists in being restrained in body, restrained in speech, and restrained in mind—that is the non-doing of evil deeds in the future.
Thus, through the wearing away of old kamma by means of asceticism and the non-doing of new kamma, there is no further influx in the future.

With no further influx in the future, there is the destruction of kamma. With the destruction of kamma, there is the destruction of suffering. With the destruction of suffering, there is the destruction of feeling. With the destruction of feeling, all suffering will be utterly worn away.”
"And that indeed is pleasing and acceptable to us; therefore we are satisfied.
When this was said, monks, I said to those Nigaṇṭhas:
"Friends, Nigaṇṭhas, there are these five things whose results are twofold even in this very life."
Which five? Faith,
preference, oral tradition, reasoned reflection, and acceptance of a view after contemplation—
these, friends Nigaṇṭhas, are the five things that have a twofold result in this very life.
"In that regard, what is the venerable Nigaṇṭhas' faith in their past teacher? What is their inclination? What is their oral tradition? What is their reasoned reflection?
What is their acceptance based on contemplation of views? Monks, when I speak thus, I do not see any legitimate rebuttal to my argument among those Nigaṇṭhas.
Furthermore, monks, I say this to those Nigaṇṭhas:
“What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas:
when there is intense exertion for you, intense striving, would you at that time experience intense, painful, piercing sensations born of exertion;
or when there is no intense exertion for you, no intense striving, would you at that time not experience intense, painful, piercing sensations born of exertion?”
“Friend Gotama, at whatever time we have intense exertion and intense striving, at that time we experience intense, painful, piercing sensations born of exertion;
but at whatever time we do not have intense exertion and intense striving, at that time we do not experience intense, painful, piercing sensations born of exertion.”

"Thus it seems, friends Nigaṇṭhas, that at the time when there is intense exertion and intense striving for you, at that time you would experience intense, painful, piercing sensations born of exertion;
but at the time when there is no intense exertion and no intense striving for you, at that time you would not experience intense, painful, piercing sensations born of exertion.
This being so, it is not appropriate for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare: [that they have attained final knowledge]."
“Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
Thus, through the exhaustion of old kamma by means of asceticism (tapas) and the non-performance of new kamma, there is no further influx in the future.

With no further influx in the future, there is the destruction of kamma; with the destruction of kamma, the destruction of suffering; with the destruction of suffering, the destruction of feeling; and with the destruction of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”

"Friends, Nigaṇṭhas, if at the time when you have intense exertion and intense striving, you did not experience intense, painful, sharp, and piercing sensations resulting from that exertion; and if, on the other hand,
at the time when you do not have intense exertion and intense striving, you experienced intense, painful, sharp, and piercing sensations resulting from that exertion—
then it would be appropriate for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to give such an explanation."
“Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
Thus, through the exhaustion of old kamma by means of asceticism (tapas) and the non-performance of new kamma, there is no further influx in the future;

with no further influx in the future, there is the destruction of kamma; with the destruction of kamma, there is the destruction of suffering; with the destruction of suffering, there is the destruction of feeling; and with the destruction of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”
But because, friends Nigaṇṭhas, at the time when there is intense exertion and intense striving for you, at that time you experience intense, painful, piercing sensations born of exertion;
yet at the time when there is no intense exertion and no intense striving for you, at that time you do not experience intense, painful, piercing sensations born of exertion—
it is while experiencing those very intense, painful, piercing sensations born of exertion yourselves that, being ignorant, unknowing, and deluded, you undergo the result.
“Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
Thus, through the exhaustion of old kamma by means of asceticism (tapas) and the non-performance of new kamma, there is no further influx in the future.

With no further influx in the future, there is the destruction of kamma; with the destruction of kamma, the destruction of suffering; with the destruction of suffering, the destruction of feeling; and with the destruction of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”
"Even when I speak thus, monks, I do not see any legitimate counter-argument among the Nigaṇṭhas.
Furthermore, monks, I say this to those Nigaṇṭhas:
'What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas, is it possible that an action to be experienced in the present life could, through effort or exertion, become an action to be experienced in a future life?'"
‘No, friend.
‘But can it be obtained that this karma, which is to be experienced in a future life, should instead be experienced in the present life through effort or exertion?
‘No, friend.’
“What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas, is it possible that this karma which is to be experienced as pleasant might, through effort or exertion, become karma to be experienced as painful?
“No, friend.
“But is it possible that this karma which is to be experienced as painful might, through effort or exertion, become karma to be experienced as pleasant?”
‘No indeed, friend.

‘What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas, regarding this action that is to be experienced when fully ripened—is it possible, through effort or exertion, for it to become something to be experienced before it has fully ripened?
‘No indeed, friend.’
"But as for this karma that is to be experienced when unripened, is it possible by means of exertion or striving to make it something to be experienced when ripened?
"No, friend.

"What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas: as for this karma that is to be experienced in great measure, is it possible by means of exertion or striving to make it something to be experienced in small measure?"
‘No, friend.
‘But is it possible that this karma, which is to be experienced little, might—through effort or exertion—become karma to be experienced much?
‘No, friend.’
“What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas: is it possible that this karma which is to be experienced can, through effort or exertion, become not to be experienced?
“No, friend.
“But is it possible that this karma which is not to be experienced can, through effort or exertion, become to be experienced?”
‘No, friend.

‘So it seems, friend Nigaṇṭhas, that it is impossible for this karma that is to be experienced in the present life to be made into karma to be experienced in a future life through effort or exertion; but as for this karma that is to be experienced in a future life…’
It is impossible by means of effort or exertion to make that which is to be experienced in the present life instead [be experienced later];
it is impossible by means of effort or exertion to make that karma which is to be experienced as pleasant instead [be experienced] as painful;
it is impossible by means of effort or exertion to make that karma which is to be experienced as painful instead [be experienced] as pleasant.
It is impossible that this karma, which is to be experienced when fully ripened, should become something to be experienced before it is fully ripened through effort or exertion;
it is impossible that this karma, which is to be experienced before it is fully ripened, should become something to be experienced only when fully ripened through effort or exertion;
it is impossible that this karma, which is to be experienced in great measure, should [be altered] through effort...
It is impossible that this karma which is to be experienced with little feeling should, through effort or exertion, become to be experienced with much feeling;
it is impossible that this karma which is to be experienced with much feeling should, through effort or exertion, become to be experienced with little feeling;

it is impossible that this karma which is to be experienced [with feeling] should, through effort or exertion, become not to be experienced; and it is impossible that this karma which is not to be experienced...
“Whether it be through effort or exertion, it is impossible for that [kamma] to become experienced [in this life];
such being the case, the effort of the venerable Nigaṇṭhas is fruitless, their exertion is fruitless.
Thus, monks, do the Nigaṇṭhas speak.
“Bhikkhus, for those Nigaṇṭhas who speak thus, ten legitimate criticisms bring them to a state of reproach.
If beings experience pleasure and pain as the result of what was done in the past,
then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas must have performed evil deeds in the past, since they now experience such painful, sharp, and bitter feelings.”
“Bhikkhus, if beings experience pleasure and pain on account of the creative act of a Supreme Lord,
then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas have been created by an evil Supreme Lord, since they now experience such painful, sharp, and bitter sensations. If, bhikkhus,
beings experience pleasure and pain on account of a collective destiny...”
"Indeed, monks, the Nigaṇṭhas have formed an evil association, since they now experience such painful, sharp, and bitter sensations. Monks,
if beings experience pleasure and pain on account of their birth,
then indeed the Nigaṇṭhas are of evil birth, since they now experience such painful, sharp, and bitter sensations."
“Bhikkhus, if beings experience pleasure and pain on account of exertion in this very life,
then surely the Nigaṇṭhas must have performed such exertion in this very life that they now experience such painful, sharp, and bitter feelings. Bhikkhus,
if beings experience pleasure and pain on account of what was done in the past, then the Nigaṇṭhas deserve censure.”
If beings do not experience pleasure and pain as the result of past deeds, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be censured.
If, monks, beings experience pleasure and pain as the result of the creation of a Supreme Lord, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be censured;
if beings do not experience pleasure and pain as the result of the creation of a Supreme Lord, the Nigaṇṭhas are still to be censured.
“Bhikkhus, if beings experience pleasure and pain because of their association with others, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be censured;
if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of their association with others, the Nigaṇṭhas are still to be censured.
If beings experience pleasure and pain because of their birth-status, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be censured.”
If beings do not experience pleasure and pain on account of their birth, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be censured.
Monks, if beings experience pleasure and pain on account of exertion in this very life, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be censured;
and if beings do not experience pleasure and pain on account of exertion in this very life, the Nigaṇṭhas are still to be censured.
“Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas speak thus.
Monks, for the Nigaṇṭhas who speak thus, these ten legitimate criticisms and rebukes come to be a ground for censure.
In this way, monks, effort becomes fruitless; striving becomes fruitless.”
And how, monks, is effort fruitful, is striving fruitful?

Here, monks, a monk does not overwhelm himself with suffering because he is not overwhelmed [by it], yet he does not relinquish the happiness that accords with the Dhamma, nor is he infatuated with that happiness.
He understands thus:

‘For me, as I exerted myself regarding this source of suffering, dispassion arose through that exertion; yet for me, as I looked on with equanimity at this source of suffering and cultivated equanimity, dispassion arose.
Thus, in whatever source of suffering dispassion arose through exertion, he exerted himself there;
and in whatever source of suffering dispassion arose through looking on with equanimity and cultivating equanimity, he cultivated equanimity there.
For one who exerts effort regarding the formation of each respective source of suffering, through that exertion of formation,
dispassion arises— and in this way, that suffering of his is worn away.
For one who looks on with equanimity toward each respective source of suffering, cultivating equanimity, dispassion arises.
In this way, too, that suffering of his is worn away.
Just as if, monks, a man were infatuated with a woman, his mind bound to her, with intense desire and intense longing;
and he were to see that woman standing, conversing, laughing, and joking with another man.
“What do you think, bhikkhus, would sorrow,
lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in that man upon seeing that woman standing, chatting, laughing, and joking with another man?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“And for what reason?
“Because, Bhante, that man is infatuated with that woman, his mind is bound to her, and he has intense desire and intense longing for her.
Therefore, seeing that woman standing, conversing, laughing, and joking with another man, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would arise in him.”
“Then, monks, it might occur to that man:
‘I am indeed infatuated with this woman, my mind is bound to her, and I have intense desire and intense longing for her.
When I see this woman standing, conversing, laughing, and joking with another man, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in me.’”
‘What if I were to abandon that desire and lust for this woman? He would then abandon that desire and lust for her.
Later on, he might see that woman standing, conversing, laughing, and joking with another man.
“What do you think, bhikkhus, would sorrow,
lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in that man upon seeing that woman standing, conversing, laughing, and joking with another man?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“And why is that? “Because, venerable sir, that man has no passion for that woman.
Therefore, seeing her standing with another man, conversing with him, laughing with him, and joking with him, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise in him.”

“In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not overwhelm himself with suffering because he has not overwhelmed himself [with worldly things], yet he does not abandon righteous happiness, nor is he infatuated with that happiness.
He understands thus:

‘When I apply effort to formations for the sake of this source of suffering, dispassion comes about through that application of effort; but when I maintain equanimity toward this source of suffering, dispassion comes about through the cultivation of equanimity.’”

Thus, for whatever source of suffering there is, when one exerts effort regarding formations, dispassion arises through that exertion of formations; one exerts effort toward that [source] regarding formations.
But for whatever source of suffering there is, when one maintains equanimity and develops equanimity, dispassion arises through that equanimity; one develops equanimity toward that [source].
For each respective source of suffering, when one exerts effort regarding formations, dispassion arises through that exertion of formations.
In this way, too, that suffering of his is worn away.
By looking on with equanimity at each source of suffering and developing equanimity toward it, dispassion arises—
in this way, too, that suffering of his is worn away.
In this way too, monks, effort is fruitful and striving is fruitful.
Furthermore, monks, a monk reflects thus:
"While I am dwelling according to my pleasure, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline."
‘But when I exert myself for my own suffering, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
What if I were to exert myself for my own suffering?
Thus, he exerts himself for his own suffering.
As he exerts himself for the sake of suffering, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
At a later time, he no longer exerts himself for the sake of suffering.
For what reason?
For that purpose for which, monks, that bhikkhu would exert himself to his own suffering, that purpose has already been accomplished;
therefore, he does not exert himself to his own suffering at a later time.
Just as, monks, a fletcher heats and warms a shaft between two fires to make it straight and workable.
But when, monks, the fletcher has heated and thoroughly warmed his arrow-shaft between two flames and made it straight and workable,
at a later time that fletcher does not again heat and thoroughly warm the arrow-shaft between two flames to make it straight and workable.
For what reason?
Because, monks, whatever purpose the fletcher had for which he would heat, scorch, straighten, and make workable the arrow-shaft between two fires—that purpose has been accomplished.
Therefore, at a later time, the fletcher does not again heat, scorch, straighten, or make workable the arrow-shaft between two fires.
In the same way, monks, a monk reflects thus:
“While I am dwelling at ease, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline;
but when I exert myself with painful effort, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase.”
‘What if I were to exert myself for my own suffering?
He exerts himself for his own suffering.
As he exerts himself for his own suffering, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
Thus, at a later time, he does not exert himself for his own suffering.
Why is that? Because, monks, whatever purpose for which that monk might have exerted himself for his own suffering, that purpose has already been accomplished.
Therefore, at a later time, he does not exert himself for his own suffering.
In this way too, monks, the effort is fruitful; the striving is fruitful.

Furthermore, monks, here a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Well-Gone One, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Thus, having realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Endowed with that attainment of faith, he reflects thus:
“The household life is crowded, a path of dust; going forth is the open air.”
"It is not easy for one living in a household to lead the holy life (brahmacariya) that is entirely complete, entirely pure, and polished like a conch shell.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Then, at a later time, having abandoned a small or a great mass of wealth, he went forth.
Having abandoned a small circle of relatives or a large circle of relatives, having shaved off hair and beard and donned saffron robes, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus, he abandons the taking of life; from the taking of life...
He abstains from taking life; he lays aside the rod and the sword, and dwells conscientious and compassionate, sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a heart free from theft, pure and clean.
Having abandoned unchastity, he lives a life of chastity; he dwells aloof, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the common practice of the village.
Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks the truth, is devoted to truth, is trustworthy, reliable, and does not deceive the world.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech;

having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people, nor having heard something there, does he repeat it here for the purpose of dividing those people—thus, among those who are divided...
He is a reconciler of those who are at variance or a promoter of friendships; he delights in harmony, rejoices in harmony, and finds joy in harmony; he speaks words that create concord.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-warming, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people.

Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Vinaya. He utters speech that is worth treasuring—timely, reasoned, measured, and connected with the goal.
He abstains from damaging seeds and plants.
He eats only one meal a day, refraining from eating at night and abstaining from food outside the proper time.
He abstains from dancing, singing, music, and witnessing theatrical performances.
He abstains from wearing garlands, using perfumes and cosmetics, and engaging in beautifying and adorning himself.
He abstains from high and luxurious beds and seats.
He abstains from accepting gold and silver.
He abstains from accepting raw grain.
He abstains from accepting raw meat.
He abstains from accepting women and girls.
He abstains from accepting male and female slaves.
He abstains from accepting goats and sheep.
He abstains from accepting chickens and pigs;
he abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares;
he abstains from accepting fields and land.
He abstains from engaging in running messages and errands.
He abstains from buying and selling.
He abstains from cheating with false weights, false metals, and false measures.
He abstains from suborning, deceiving, cheating, and crooked practices.
He abstains from cutting, killing, binding, robbing, plundering, and acts of violence.
He is content with robes that suffice for his body and almsfood that suffice for his belly. Wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these things with him.

Just as a winged bird, wherever it flies, flies with its wings as its only burden, even so a bhikkhu is content with robes to protect the body and almsfood to sustain the belly; wherever he goes, he goes having taken these along.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the happiness that is blameless.
Thus, having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of the eye and attains mastery over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue … [and so forth] …
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
[and so on] ...having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary details.
For if one dwells with this faculty of the mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—[arise].
If unwholesome states were to flow into him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the faculty of the mind and attains mastery over the faculty of the mind.
Endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself the untainted happiness.
Whether moving forward or backward, he acts with clear comprehension; whether looking ahead or looking aside, he acts with clear comprehension.
He acts with clear comprehension when bending and extending his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension in carrying his outer robe, bowl, and inner robe;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension in defecating and urinating;
and he acts with clear comprehension when going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
Thus, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, endowed with this noble contentment,
endowed with this noble restraint of the sense faculties, and endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension,
he resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Then, having returned from his alms round after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind calmed within; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, free from indecision regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.

Thus, having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
In this way too, monks, the effort is fruitful; the striving is fruitful.

Furthermore, monks, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is internal tranquility and unification of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness.
In this way too, monks, the effort is fruitful; the striving is fruitful.
Furthermore, monks, with the fading away of rapture, a monk dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
And he experiences pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: "He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous.
In this way too, monks, the effort is fruitful, the striving is fruitful.
Furthermore, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
In this way too, monks, effort is fruitful and striving is fruitful.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from blemish, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say, one birth, two births, three births... four births... five births... ten births... twenty births... thirty births... forty births... fifty births... a hundred births... a thousand births... a hundred thousand births... many aeons of world-contraction... many aeons of world-expansion... many aeons of world-contraction and expansion... Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and particulars.
Whether four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births,
a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, or many aeons of world-contraction,
many aeons of world-expansion, or many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion: “In that place I was...”
‘I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose elsewhere; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I was reborn here. Thus, with its aspects and particulars, he recollects his manifold past lives.
He recollects his past lives.
In this way too, monks, the undertaking is fruitful, the striving is fruitful.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—
low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma:
"Alas, these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct in body, misconduct in speech, and misconduct in mind..."
These beings were possessed of wrong view, revilers of the noble ones, holders of false views, and undertakers of actions based on false views;
at the breaking up of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But these worthy beings were possessed of good conduct of body, possessed of good conduct of speech, and possessed of good conduct of mind.
‘They do not revile the noble ones; they hold right view and undertake actions based on right view.

With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate.
He understands beings according to their deeds.
In this way too, monks, the undertaking is fruitful, the striving is fruitful.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from blemish, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
Thus one understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; one understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; one understands as it really is:
"This is the cessation of suffering"; one understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
He understands as it really is: “These are the taints”; he understands as it really is: “This is the origin of the taints”;
he understands as it really is: “This is the cessation of the taints”; he understands as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.”

For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When it is liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated.
One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
"Thus indeed, monks, effort is fruitful; thus indeed, striving is fruitful.
Such is the teaching of the Tathāgatas, monks.
For those Tathāgatas who teach thus, ten grounds for praise consistent with the Dhamma arise."
“Bhikkhus, if beings experience pleasure and pain as a result of what was done in the past,
then surely the Tathāgata must have performed well-done deeds in the past, since he now experiences such taintless pleasant feelings. Bhikkhus,
if beings experience pleasure and pain as a result of the creation of a Supreme Lord...”
"Indeed, monks, the Tathāgata has been fashioned by a fortunate lord, since he now experiences such taintless, pleasant feelings. Monks,
if beings experience pleasure and pain because of their association with others,
then indeed the Tathāgata has a virtuous association, since he now experiences such taintless, pleasant feelings."
“Bhikkhus, if beings experience pleasure and pain because of their noble birth,
then surely the Tathāgata is of noble birth, since he now experiences such taintless pleasant feelings. Bhikkhus,
if beings experience pleasure and pain because of their exertion in the present life...”
"Indeed, monks, the Tathāgata has successfully applied himself to the Dhamma in this very life, since he now experiences such taintless pleasant feelings.
Whether beings experience pleasure and pain as the result of past deeds, monks, the Tathāgata is praiseworthy;
or if beings do not experience pleasure and pain as the result of past deeds, the Tathāgata is still praiseworthy."
“Bhikkhus, if beings experience pleasure and pain caused by the creative act of a Supreme God (issaranimmāna), the Tathāgata is to be praised;
if beings do not experience pleasure and pain caused by the creative act of a Supreme God, the Tathāgata is to be praised.
If beings experience pleasure and pain caused by chance (saṅgatibhāva), the Tathāgata is to be praised.”
If beings do not experience pleasure and pain on account of their coming together, the Tathāgata is to be praised.
If, monks, beings experience pleasure and pain on account of their birth-status, the Tathāgata is to be praised;
if beings do not experience pleasure and pain on account of their birth-status, the Tathāgata is to be praised.
“Bhikkhus, whether beings experience pleasure and pain because of exertion in this very life, the Tathāgata is to be praised;
or if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of exertion in this very life, the Tathāgata is still to be praised.
Such is the teaching of the Tathāgatas, bhikkhus.”
“Bhikkhus, for Tathāgatas who speak thus, these ten grounds for praise in accordance with the Dhamma come to pass.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Devadaha Sutta is finished; the first.
